overview.text: César Chávez (1927–1993) was a Mexican American labor and civil-rights organizer who became a prominent leader of the farmworker movement. After growing up doing migrant farm labor, he left the Community Service Organization to focus on organizing agricultural workers. In 1962, he and Dolores Huerta, with other organizers, formed the National Farm Workers Association (NFWA). During the 1965 Delano Grape Strike, the NFWA joined Filipino farmworkers organized by Larry Itliong; the groups later united in the organization that became the United Farm Workers (UFW). Chávez helped lead strikes, marches, consumer boycotts, and fasts to press for better wages and working conditions, bringing farmworkers’ concerns to national attention. His work connected labor organizing with Latino civil-rights activism.

key_facts.text: Chávez was born near Yuma, Arizona, in 1927, and experienced migrant farm labor after leaving school following eighth grade.
In 1962, Chávez, Dolores Huerta, and other organizers formed the National Farm Workers Association, a predecessor to the UFW.
The 1965 Delano Grape Strike began with Filipino farmworkers organized by Larry Itliong; Chávez’s NFWA joined their strike.
The movement used nonviolent tactics including strikes, marches, consumer boycotts, and fasts to draw attention to farmworkers’ conditions.
Chávez died in Arizona in 1993; his organizing helped make farmworker rights a major public issue.
